gastronomy:Mercat de la Boqueria.name: Mercat de la Boqueria
gastronomy:Mercat de la Boqueria.teaser: Skip the fruit cups at the Rambla front: the trading floor starts three rows back
gastronomy:Mercat de la Boqueria.story: Stalls have stood here since 1840, on ground cleared when the Convent of Sant Josep came down. The first rows off La Rambla are dressed for visitors, with fruit cups and paper cones of ham; walk past them and the market changes, men in rubber aprons gutting fish and cheese wheels stacked to the shoulder. Look for Garrotxa and Serrat Gros goat cheeses, bellota ham carved to order, figs and tomatoes in their weeks, salted anchovies from L'Escala. One counter is gone: Pinotxo, Juanito Bayén's bar since 1940, left after his death in 2023; Bar Central still serves at the back.
gastronomy:Mercat de la Boqueria.why: Go early, eat a counter breakfast at the back, and buy cheese before the tour groups arrive.
facts: Monday to Saturday, closed Sunday; many fish stalls shut on Monday (Oct 2026)
Before 11:00, ahead of the lunchtime crush
Garrotxa and Serrat Gros cheese, bellota ham, L'Escala anchovies, figs in late summer

gastronomy:Mercat de Sant Antoni.name: Mercat de Sant Antoni
gastronomy:Mercat de Sant Antoni.teaser: An 1882 iron market shaped like a cross, with a Sunday ring of old books around it
gastronomy:Mercat de Sant Antoni.story: Antoni Rovira i Trias drew a plan for the whole Eixample and lost the commission to Ildefons Cerdà; the city gave him this market instead, a cast-iron cross finished in 1882 that fills an entire block. It closed in 2010 for a restoration that ran eight years, and reopened in 2018 with the food halls back under the iron. On Sunday mornings the stalls around the outside sell second-hand books, comics, old coins and football cards, and the neighbourhood drifts from there to vermut. Pinotxo, the famous counter that left the Boqueria, reopened here in 2023, on the Comte d'Urgell and Tamarit corner.
gastronomy:Mercat de Sant Antoni.why: Do the Sunday book stalls first, then cross the street for a vermut: that is the local Sunday.

gastronomy:Mercat de Santa Caterina.name: Mercat de Santa Caterina
gastronomy:Mercat de Santa Caterina.teaser: A wave of 67 colours over the stalls, each tile a fruit or vegetable sold underneath
gastronomy:Mercat de Santa Caterina.story: The Dominicans built a convent here in 1243; it was pulled down in 1837 and a market took its place. Between 1997 and 2005 Enric Miralles and Benedetta Tagliabue rebuilt it under a roof that rolls like a sea swell, covered with some 325,000 ceramic hexagons in 67 colours, the palette taken from the produce on the counters below. Miralles died in 2000, before it opened; Tagliabue finished the job. Inside it is smaller and calmer than the Boqueria, a neighbourhood market for the Born, and at the back excavated walls of the old convent sit under glass.
gastronomy:Mercat de Santa Caterina.why: See the roof from a terrace or upper window nearby, then shop inside where the Born actually buys.
facts: Mid-morning on a weekday, when the stalls are full and the crowds are thin (check hours)

provisioning:Casa Gispert.name: Casa Gispert
provisioning:Casa Gispert.teaser: Almonds and hazelnuts roasted over oak in the back, weighed on brass scales at the front
provisioning:Casa Gispert.story: Behind Santa Maria del Mar, on Carrer dels Sombrerers, a shop has roasted nuts since 1851 in a wood-fired oven at the back, which it calls the oldest of its kind still working in Europe. The almonds and hazelnuts go in whole, come out warm and faintly smoky, and are weighed by hand at the wooden counter, not sold pre-bagged. The Gispert family ran it from 1911; the Margenat brothers took over in 1993, and Enric Comelles and Gemma Marín have kept it since 2013. In 1999 a French gourmets' society gave it the Coq d'Or for Europe's best roasted nuts.
provisioning:Casa Gispert.why: Buy a bag of the warm oak-roasted almonds for the boat: there are no seats, just the counter and the smell.
facts: Carrer dels Sombrerers 23, El Born, behind Santa Maria del Mar

gastronomy:Formatgeria La Seu.name: Formatgeria La Seu
gastronomy:Formatgeria La Seu.teaser: A narrow Gòtic shop that sells only Spanish and Catalan farm cheese, cut while you taste
gastronomy:Formatgeria La Seu.story: On Carrer de la Dagueria, a lane off Via Laietana in the Barri Gòtic, a Scottish cheesemonger, Katherine McLaughlin, built a small room around Spanish farmhouse cheese. The counter runs from Catalan goat's milk, Garrotxa and its ash-coated sister Garrotxa Negra, to Pyrenean Tupí, a fermented cheese spread sharp with brandy, and raw-milk Manchego and Mahón from further off, with Mont d'Or in winter. You are expected to taste before buying, and the person behind the counter will ask what you are serving it with.
gastronomy:Formatgeria La Seu.why: Ask for a tasting of three Catalan goat cheeses and buy the one that suits the boat's next lunch.

gastronomy:Entre Latas · Conservas Gourm.name: Entre Latas
gastronomy:Entre Latas · Conservas Gourm.teaser: A former wine cellar in Gràcia stocked with nothing but tins, and vermut from the barrel
gastronomy:Entre Latas · Conservas Gourm.story: Time Out calls it the first shop in Barcelona given over entirely to tinned food. It fills an old wine cellar on Carrer de Torrijos, near Joanic, and Paola Fornasaro stocks it with Cantabrian anchovies, Galician zamburiñas and cockles and odd imports, some 500 references from a dozen-odd countries. A few stools and toasts mean you can open a tin on the spot with bread and a glass of red or white vermut drawn from the barrel, as the cellar always did. The serious buyers treat old vintage tins the way others treat wine.

gastronomy:Recaredo — biodynamic Corpinn.name: Recaredo
gastronomy:Recaredo — biodynamic Corpinn.teaser: A family cellar in Sant Sadurní where every bottle is disgorged by hand
gastronomy:Recaredo — biodynamic Corpinn.story: A family house on Carrer Tamarit in Sant Sadurní, Recaredo makes only its own estate wine. In 2010 Recaredo became the first sparkling house in the region certified biodynamic by Demeter. Every bottle ages under natural cork rather than a crown cap and is disgorged by hand; no sulphites are added. In 2019 it left DO Cava with the growers who founded Corpinnat. Its single-hectare Turó d'en Mota, old Xarel·lo vines given years on the lees, is the bottle collectors chase. Visits now end with a taste of L'Infinit, a newer family project, from February 2026.
gastronomy:Recaredo — biodynamic Corpinn.why: Book the cellar visit for the hand-disgorging rather than the shop: you see a craft most houses gave up.

gastronomy:Gramona — Corpinnat.name: Gramona
gastronomy:Gramona — Corpinnat.teaser: Five generations since 1881, and sparkling wines left to age on their yeast for fifteen years
gastronomy:Gramona — Corpinnat.story: Gramona has made wine in Sant Sadurní since 1881 and is now in its fifth family generation. The house is known for patience: Tres Lustros, its name meaning three five-year spans, rests on its lees for more than 180 months before release. The vineyards have been Demeter-certified biodynamic since 2014, the cellars run on geothermal energy, and rainwater is collected. It left DO Cava in 2019 to found Corpinnat. A full visit starts at the old house on Carrer Indústria, crosses to the newer Celler Batlle on the edge of town, and returns to the deep cellars where the longest wines sleep.
gastronomy:Gramona — Corpinnat.why: Taste an old Gramona beside a young one: the gap shows what time on the lees does.
facts: Carrer Indústria 36, Sant Sadurní d'Anoia; Celler Batlle on the edge of town

gastronomy:Bodegas Yzaguirre — Reus 1884.name: Bodegas Yzaguirre
gastronomy:Bodegas Yzaguirre — Reus 1884.teaser: The vermut founded in Reus in 1884, still made to a secret herb formula near Tarragona
gastronomy:Bodegas Yzaguirre — Reus 1884.story: Enrique de Yzaguirre y de Basterreche started the house in Reus in 1884, and it calls itself Spain's first commercial vermut. The recipe, around 80 herbs, roots and spices, is kept a trade secret. Today the Salla-Solé family owns it, and the wine is made at El Morell, just north of Tarragona, where new buildings opened in 2025 with a guided visit, the Yzaguirre Experience: the brand's Reus origins, the botanicals, the barrels where the reserves age, then a tasting. In Barcelona it is the bottle you see behind the counter at the old vermut bars; those bars have their own cards in the tables.
gastronomy:Bodegas Yzaguirre — Reus 1884.why: Taste the barrel-aged reserva beside the everyday red, and the difference explains the bars' loyalty.
facts: Carretera de Valls C-14 km 9.5, El Morell (Tarragona), about an hour south

around:Montserrat.name: Montserrat
around:Montserrat.teaser: A Benedictine abbey on a ledge of a sawtooth massif, and a boys' choir at one o'clock
around:Montserrat.story: Montserrat means the sawn mountain, and from the train you see why: a ridge of rounded conglomerate fingers rising to about 1,236 m. The Benedictine abbey clings to a ledge at 720 m, home to La Moreneta, the dark wooden Virgin who is Catalonia's patron. Time the trip for the Escolania, one of Europe's oldest boys' choirs, which sings in the basilica at 13:00 on weekdays and at noon on Sundays. The boys are away on Saturdays, through the summer holidays and around Christmas, so check before you go. Then climb past the abbey on the paths along the cliffs.
around:Montserrat.why: Hear the Escolania sing in the basilica: it is the reason to time the whole day.

around:Sitges.name: Sitges
around:Sitges.teaser: A whitewashed seaside town where a painter hung El Grecos and a sweet wine paid for the hospital
around:Sitges.story: Sitges was where Catalan modernism spent its summers. Santiago Rusiñol, painter and writer, made Cau Ferrat, his studio and collection, and filled it with wrought iron, two El Grecos and three Picassos; it is a museum now, next to the church that stands over the sea. The town's other story is in the glass: Malvasia de Sitges, a sweet golden white grown here since the Middle Ages, whose sales long kept the local hospital going, and which the town keeps alive with its own interpretation centre. Then the beaches, a few steps from the station.
around:Sitges.why: See Cau Ferrat, then drink a glass of Malvasia de Sitges, the wine almost nobody outside the town knows.

around:Colònia Güell.name: Colònia Güell
around:Colònia Güell.teaser: The workers' village where Gaudí hung strings and weights to find the Sagrada Família's shape
around:Colònia Güell.story: In the late 19th century the Güell textile mill at Santa Coloma de Cervelló was given a modernist colony for its workers, and Gaudí was asked to design its church. From 1898 he spent about ten years modelling it upside down, strings hung with weights so that gravity drew the curves: the poly-funicular model. Only the crypt was built, its leaning columns and brick vaults the trial run for ideas he then took to the Sagrada Família. It joined the UNESCO Gaudí listing in 2005, and on a weekday you may have it almost to yourself.
around:Colònia Güell.why: This is the quietest Gaudí you will see, and the one that explains how the others stand up.

around:Penedès — Sant Sadurní and the ca.name: Penedès and Sant Sadurní
around:Penedès — Sant Sadurní and the ca.teaser: An hour of vines and chalky soil, and a modernist cathedral of cava under the ground
around:Penedès — Sant Sadurní and the ca.story: Take the R4 for 45 minutes and you are in the town that makes most of Spain's sparkling wine: about 95 percent of all cava comes from this small patch of Penedès. The grand visit is Codorníu, whose cellars Josep Puig i Cadafalch built between 1895 and 1921, arches and tunnels running for kilometres under the vines, now a national monument. Freixenet sits beside the station. Vilafranca del Penedès, a stop further, is the still-wine capital. The newer story is the growers farming the same chalk with fewer interventions and natural ferments; Recaredo and Gramona have their own cards.
around:Penedès — Sant Sadurní and the ca.why: Do Codorníu's cellars for the architecture, then one small grower for what is in the glass now.

around:Montseny.name: Montseny
around:Montseny.teaser: Beech woods, Europe's southernmost firs, and autumn menus built on mushrooms and chestnuts
around:Montseny.story: An hour north the land rises to Turó de l'Home at 1,706 m, through holm oak, then beech, then the fir forest that is the southernmost of its kind in Europe. That forest is largely why UNESCO named the Montseny a biosphere reserve in 1978. On a clear day from the top you look back over Tibidabo to the sea. Autumn is the season to come: the beeches turn copper, people walk out with baskets, and the village restaurants put wild mushrooms and chestnuts on everything. It is a protected landscape with farms still working it, not a theme park.
around:Montseny.why: Come in October or November and eat the mushroom menu in a village restaurant.

Girona is a medieval river city: houses painted ochre and rust stacked over the Onyar, one of Europe's best-kept Jewish quarters in the Call, and a Gothic cathedral at the top of a long flight of steps. On the edge of town the Roca brothers run El Celler de Can Roca, which held three MICHELIN stars in the 2026 guide. We tell the city properly in its own guide.

around:Costa Brava — Camí de Ronda.teaser: The old smugglers' patrol path, cove to cove from Calella de Palafrugell to Aiguablava
around:Costa Brava — Camí de Ronda.story: The Baix Empordà coast, Calella de Palafrugell, Begur, Aiguablava, is stitched together by the Camí de Ronda, a cliff path through pine and coves. around:Cadaqués & Cap de Creus.teaser: Mainland Spain's eastern tip: twisted schist, white houses and Dalí's house at Portlligat

avoid-traps:Visiting in August.name: Barcelona in August
avoid-traps:Visiting in August.teaser: Peak heat, peak crowds, and the family kitchens shut for their holidays
avoid-traps:Visiting in August.story: In August many of the family-run Catalan restaurants and small bodegas close for a fortnight or longer, Bar Tomás in Sarrià among them, just as the heat and the crowds reach their highest. The exceptions are the neighbourhood festes: Gràcia in mid-August, with streets the neighbours decorate themselves, and Sants straight after. Otherwise the city is at its best from April to June and in September and October.
avoid-traps:Visiting in August.why: Come in spring or autumn; if it must be August, aim for the Gràcia or Sants festes.
facts: Check that the restaurant you want is open before planning around it in August
